utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. One procedural matter. I was informed that the Defence would like to hand out a summary of the last motion to Mr. Krajisnik. Is this to inform him or just to give details, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's to keep our client informed, Your Honour; it's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was not informed until now about this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that isn't what I said at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I asked -- yes, okay. I'm just trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour, and I'm clarifying as well. Of course we keep him informed but we would like to update the information, Your Honour, and that's what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any problem? No problem so the request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, perhaps is the Prosecution intending to respond to this motion? The last motion filed by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are considering it, Your Honour. We received it yesterday and we are probably going to respond to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any idea about timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We don't, Your Honour. I will be able to inform the Court perhaps at the end of the day when we have a chance to consult on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So that we can dispose it -- dispose of the -- to deal with it and decide on the motion without delay. Then the next small issue, procedural issue I would like to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I again remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Stewart you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, good morning. I feel like a sort of deputy headmaster. I wonder what progress you were able to make with the homework on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed about that. Mr. Registrar has been provided with the result of your homework, Mr. Krajisnik. That is, same map, different marking on it. I see that the original is returned. Perhaps it would be a good idea -- oh, I see that even a computerised version is -- well, as a matter of fact, I invited you, Mr. Krajisnik, to -- not to make any further markings but on one of the copies I see that more or less the whole of the strategic goals are laid out. That means if I could say the corridor between Semberija and Krajina indicated, the corridor from Semberija to Romanija indicated, the -- it does not say anything specific about the Drina river but that's understandable on the basis of your testimony, and then we see the Neretva River issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, may I just inquire? I'm not sure -- it sounds as if Your Honour is looking at a piece of material that we haven't yet seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then, I should give it to you because we now have different version of marked maps. Well, we have a lot by now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did what you assigned me to do. This is the original map and this is a contribution for further understanding. I did not add anything to your map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I do see -- I suggest the following. Could this be shown to the -- Madam Usher, could this be shown to the parties? Yes. And could this be shown to the parties as well? If you give that to the Prosecution, then this one to the Defence, please, and then to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber suggests the following to the parties. The map as I marked it yesterday, to have it admitted in order to better understand the testimony of yesterday, therefore we can't miss it, not because it's such a beautiful map. Then to add to that, same size, the map on which Mr. Krajisnik clearly indicated the -- where approximately the corridor would have to be. Mr. Krajisnik made some other -- some markings on the same map in smaller size, also including other parts, I take it, from the strategic goals. The Chamber leaves it to the parties to what extent they would like to have that admitted into evidence as well, because it certainly would need -- there are quite a lot of arrows which have not been part of the testimony until now so if you'd like to further explore that, the Chamber will not at this moment insist on it. You could use that material prepared by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one quick question. The Court referred to the document marked by Mr. Krajisnik. I take it that was a document that was marked yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. This is the one I marked yesterday. That would then be [indiscernible] C2. That would then become C2A and then the map exactly the same map on which Mr. Krajisnik indicated in red in more detail there my idea on where the corridor would be is clarified to make that C2B and whatever of the other markings you'd like to use or have explained by Mr. Krajisnik, you're free to do so. Did you receive copies of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did, and in the immediate run-up to court we hadn't actually appreciated that there were three other items attached to the piece of paper. Your Honour, I'm -- I'm more than -- more than happy with Your Honour's suggestion, which -- because it's clear from the transcript what the provenance of that C2B map is. Your Honour, I was going to suggest though that, yes, indeed it will be appropriate to seek explanation from Mr. Krajisnik on the other three documents that he's received -- he's prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So those -- well, at some convenient point those have should have an appropriate D exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it up to you to what extent you would like to deal with that. Then I add to that, there is another map, which, from what I see from the Cyrillic, is a marked Cutileiro, but -- at least it's related to Cutileiro although it's not exactly the same as what we saw before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- would Your Honour please hold that up just for a second? I think that may be one of the items that we -- yes, it seems to be, Your Honour. That is -- I mentioned we received a clip of items, and the first -- of the four items I've got the first one is the smaller version what C2B, recalling Your Honour's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we've got the same -- the second item is the same reduced map marked in a different way, with different red lines. The next one is the same map again, marked in a further different way with red lines and black arrows and then the fourth item in the little clip appears from what I can see from a few metres away, Your Honour, to be just what Your Honour was holding up a few minutes ago, the Cutileiro map marked with some red lines, arrows and, well, some sort of Pentagon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the only difference with the first map you mentioned, it's different from 2B that in 2B the marking is made by hand and here it seems to be a computerised red, but the shape is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour I'm not sure I've even just seen what's now C2B, so may I, Your Honour, glance at it just have a glance at it? It's probably not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's exactly the same but now handmade instead of computerised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour I had seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's got a tiny little bit of red against Han Pijesak but I doubt whether that's going to affect the price of fish very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the map marked by me will now be C2A and the other one will be C2B. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Has Mr. Krajisnik now got this material, Your Honour, or has he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have dealt with mine. So if any of those -- but I see that you have -- you have copies with you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can have a look. All the copies are the same like your copies. All of these were copies for me. Perhaps somebody can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have seen the copies. Let's just be sure that we know exactly on which map we are working so what markings are found on the map you're asking questions about, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I probably just need for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik has got this clip of four items. I just need to have -- I'm in Your Honour's hands but I just need to have a simple system of numbering for those four items so we with switch easily from one to the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about giving a serial number for the whole of it and then start working A, B, and C. Mr. Registrar the next number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D192, and we'll see how many you use and then we will assign A, Bs, and Cs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I were for the moment to call this clip of four documents A, B, C, D, that with make life much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have to know which one you're going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, no, no, Your Honour, physically they are in an order. We've all got them in the same order, A, B, C, D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got them loose, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps Your Honour can be given -- I've got the same thing as Mr. Krajisnik's got, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we make D192 this map 04022623, marked with only a red Semberija-Romanija corridor line, nothing else marked on it. Then the second one, same map with some eight black arrows on it, and some red markings, Krajina in the west, Posavina corridor, Romanija, Semberija corridor, one on the -- the real south of Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, the map with a lot of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the one, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one. Okay, that will be 190 -- D192B and then C is similar but the markings a bit different. One of the striking differences being that the Posavina corridor is not marked by parallel lines but by two lines coming together at the eastern part of those two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and there is a little extra line. That's the one, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And an extra line going north to the west. That will be 192C. And then the last one is a grey map with -- which is a different map but it's -- it seems that the name of Cutileiro appears on the bottom of it in Cyrillic. It's greyish and there are quite a lot of markings, red only, all the arrows in red. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm quite confident that is exactly the right stuff in the right order. And Mr. Krajisnik is nodding he has that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let's look at A then first of that clip. Now, is the position that all you have done on there by marking the computerised red line is indicate, in a slightly more refined and defined way, what was under discussion yesterday and was marked by His Honour on His Honour's map, C2A with dotted lines. So you just attempted to simplify and indicate very specifically the proposed location of that corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not proposing to ask any further question based on that map except to ask you straight away whether you feel immediately that there is any explanation that you really need to add in relation to this map at this point.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fulfilled the obligation given me by His Honour, and I tried to mark where we thought -- where we planned arbitrarily the route of the corridor, and the corridor was subject to agreement with the parties. And that was our right. So that's the corridor that goes the length of the Drina. And, of course, it was subject to talks, as far as I know, where we need territories and so on. But those here are Serb areas through which the corridor was supposed to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terribly sorry, my question is slightly naive maybe, but that corridor that you showed us as you draw it, first of all, tell us why do you need it there in an area which seems to be completely Serbian, from the colour at least, on the map. I understand that you would want to place the corridor in a non-Serbian area but why would you draw a line on a -- on the territory that seems to be absolutely Serbian? And second question, what is the status of this corridor? Does that mean that it's a road? Is it a protected road by military presence or is it a road that has a particular status? Could you please answer those two questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would appreciate it if you could put in front of you the first -- the last map, the Cutileiro map, in order to follow my explanation. The background we worked against was the Cutileiro map. That was before the armed conflict. All this inside, Romanija, et cetera, are unconnected Serb territories, just like Krajina was disconnected. Then when the armed conflict broke out, we said just like we had to take Krajina out of its isolation, we have to connect these territories, because different times had begun. So the background for our work was this map and we wanted to improve the Cutileiro plan with those corridors as a new component that emerged during the armed conflict. Therefore, the whole area was under blockade, isolated, and we wanted to save it from its isolation. That's the reason why this corridor starts, like His Honour said, on the top, where the corridor is cut off by Muslim territory, and we were saying we should exchange, swap now, so that Romanija and Birac are no longer cut off. That's the different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, did Mr. Krajisnik deal with Your Honour's second question? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I understood that there was -- there was no need nor a special status because the presence of this corridor depended on an agreement and an exchange of population. So if there is an agreement between parties, there was no need for a special party to defend the existence of this special corridor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An exchange of territories, an exchange of territories was needed in order to effect that. Like exchanges were made in order to make the Posavina corridor and the Cutileiro plan allowed for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to make sure Your Honour's question hadn't slipped through the net.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Merci.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then, can we then go to -- it's the next one, map B in this clip of maps? And I'm sticking with strategic objective 3 here at the moment, Mr. Krajisnik. I don't want to stray into the other bits of the maps that deal with the other numbered objectives. So staying with that, there is a variation here. You've -- the main line, zig-zag line north-south, appears to be exactly the same as on map A but there is added a line branching off to the northeast. Could you explain that? Well, first of all, you're clear which line I'm talking about, Mr. Krajisnik, are you? The one that runs up to the eastern border.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a sort of spur. What is the explanation of that addition by you to the map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it is necessary to look at the Cutileiro map and see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's D.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the last one. And you will see this whole area ended up in Muslim hands, although there is a connection with Serbia in this area, in the territory of not Skelani but Bratunac. Therefore, we were saying, in case we are unable to agree on an exchange of territory to connect Semberija and Majevica, Semberija and Romanija, rather, as we see on the Cutileiro map, we will demand that the corridor pass on the right side. Let me explain why Mr. Cutileiro gave this territory to the Muslim side, because it's practically their territory, their territory apart from the Cazin Krajina is compact, connected, whereas we lacked connection in this part here because Herzegovina was connected to Montenegro and therefore was not isolated. We accepted that as a compromise, namely the Muslim side would have one separate territory whereas we would have two, Krajina and Romanija. Now, when the war broke out, we took this blue-green map, the working map, reflecting our rights, in order to establish this corridor and connect Semberija with Krajina. That was the reason. So we said, if you don't want an exchange, then give us what is ours. Let us use the passage on the right-hand side in order to form a Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So to simplify, Mr. Krajisnik, from the point where that spur goes off to the northeast up to the border, the -- we are talking about alternatives, but this was the less-preferred but alternative proposal if the main proposal going right up to the north, into Semberija, could not be achieved? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first map that I drew is the basic map, and it was our goal to connect our territories in that way. We wanted to connect Serb territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina amongst themselves and as an alternative, if this should be impossible, to connect with Serbia and go through Serbia because we needed agreement with the Muslim side on this. This was just a necessary contingency plan, an alternative, and the first one is the basic option. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour that's a slightly different way of suggesting the same thing but I would suggest that that is clear and that is a clear confirmation such as I was seeking. I hope Your Honours are satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd said, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm sticking with strategic objective 3 for the moment, consequently there appears to be nothing more to be added in relation to strategic objective 3 arising from map C and D because you've already commented on D. You're content with that, Mr. Krajisnik, are you? Just so far as strategic objective 3 is concerned, there is nothing more now to be added by comment on these maps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Or rather no, no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to then -- I'm going to jog back to objective 2, apologies, we have to go backwards and forwards a little bit, for this reason, that you have included in these newly produced maps of yours, a variation, variant, as between maps B and C. I just observe that there appears to be, apart from an arrow, no significant difference between B and D but could you explain, please, the slightly more elaborate marking in the north in relation to obviously strategic objective 2 that we see on map C?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one -- no, yes. I think this second map is clear but let me explain some more. That is strategic goal 2 that was to include all three sides, the Serb, Croat and Muslim sides because we have passage from Brcko where we see this arrow and there is a section of Muslim territory there. That should be ensured through exchange, so that the corridor can pass this way. Related to this corridor, at the bottom, we see Kupres. On this point, I explained this is in the western part. I explained that Croats were interested in it because they wanted Central Bosnia connected with Croatia so I drew this arrow to show the potential exchange capacity and Croat interest in exchanging territories. In this Posavina area, we have an arrow showing Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder perhaps this map C could go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. That's great, thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you appreciate the two items that you're particularly being asked about are just where the black arrow is in the northeast, that -- sort of open -- that V-shaped addition to the east and then the almost vertical line running slightly east or north at the other end to the west that goes up to the border. Those are the two changes as between C and D so it's your explanation of each of those additions which is being sought. Take them whichever way round you like.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Posavina. And there you see there are blue areas, there are Serbs, but there is a large number of Croats as well. In the Cutileiro plan, this went to the Croat ethnic community. If you look at the last page, you will see this was Croat and we talked in Graz about two things. One is outlet to the sea. But the second one was how to ensure our corridor there. And then we showed the previous map, showing where the Muslim side would be included and this map showing where the Croat side would be included. So this is how the corridor would be resolved. How? It would go through the Serb and Croat side up to the border here. This is Muslim territory here. The missing part for us. And since there was a Croat representative at that meeting, one option -- this was Croatia. One option was to make a bridge there and in case we don't agree with the Muslims, we would have this bridge to cross to this territory here whereas Croats wanted this part here to connect Central Bosnia and, of course, these territories there are Serb. It would certainly require negotiations, including Croatia and, by necessity, the Muslim side because that would concern a change of borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. That was one option that was exploited later when we couldn't find a solution for Brcko in which both Muslims and Serbs had a vested interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm certainly not in the business of encouraging endless markings of maps but it occurs to me the that last two or three minutes - it's certainly not Mr. Krajisnik's fault - are likely to be completely incomprehensible on a later reading of the transcript. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You make it comprehensible, Mr. Stewart, either by inviting Mr. Krajisnik to mark or to describe for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm more than happy with the marking. I simply wanted to be sure Your Honour's weren't going to be resistant to further marking of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you -- as soon as you started referring to bridge and using the pointer, I am going to have to ask you, please, to make a marking on that map to indicate at each point when you refer to a specific feature or a specific point such as making a bridge there. I ask you to mark it and then we'll consider some suitable label for it. So --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that under the Cutileiro plan, this was Posavina, 1, and it went to the Croat side. You will see that on the Cutileiro plan. And then this map reflects one possibility that includes only an exchange of territory between Serbs and Croats. Then another option was found. Here, in this part, number 2, there was supposed to be a bridge, in order for the corridor to cross to Croatia, and here, number 3, there would be a bridge that would take us across to the Bosnian side. In this way -- sorry, one more thing. Number 4 is the area near Kupres the Croats were anxious to have in order to have a connection with Central Bosnia, between central Bosnia and Croatia. So that was the subject of our talks, in addition to the outlet to the sea. If we were only to talk about an exchange of territory between Serbs and Croats, and it included also those blue areas, number 5, Serb areas that would go to the Croat side. So we had the Cutileiro plan before us and we worked on this map to see whether we could compact territories and exchange territories to arrive at an acceptable solution. Under the Cutileiro plan, the number 4 was supposed to go to the Serbs but the other part here wasn't. It wasn't agreed. It was just discussed as an option. Although the primary option was one shown in the basic map. We wanted the corridor to go entirely through Bosnia and Herzegovina, without diverting into Croatia but we needed an agreement for that with the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The basic map for these purposes is map B, when you're referring to this corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you going to add an explanation, then, of the spur at the western end that runs up to the northern border? Just to the left on the page of number 5.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, up at the top, the very north?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes recognition just to the very left of where you've put your -- yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part here, where the refinery Brod was located, that's number 6, that parliament of Posavina was supposed to go to the Serb side. In our talks, that was discussed, because we told them, you have three or four refineries in Croatia and it would be fair for us to have some of the facilities too. We discussed that this line should look like this. I have to say for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that there could be some adjustments to this map. But this is what we talked about and I tried to depict the map as faithfully as I could. There could be a margin of error of 100 metres up or down but this is the -- this reflects the essence of our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we take a clean copy and leave that to be 192C, and that the marked copy will then be D192E. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I'm not going to ask you anything more on map D then in relation to strategic objective 2 or 3. Your Honour may I simply observe that although a Cutileiro map D is different from the main Cutileiro map in that it only distinguishes between Serb and non-Serb areas and so doesn't draw any distinction between Muslim and Croat areas which are all white. So one does need to look at the proper Cutileiro map for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And one of the other major difference with D7B which is the Cutileiro map in D7B we find Semberija and Romanija connected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely right, Your Honour, that difference is plainly there as well. But in terms of use of map, that -- the fact that the Croat and Muslim areas are not distinguished on that map, D, is something, well, just to watch out for, Your Honour, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Certainly. I had this copy not the other one. I'm so sorry. If necessary, I'll draw what is needed very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I don't think it matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was just so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only question arises is why the -- whether first of all D192D lacks some information which we find on D7B but, of course, the differences in connected Serb areas raises the question of whether this was an earlier stage of the negotiations or a later stage and that's, of course, still unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what I'd like to do now is just turn back to - I hope you still have it there - the minute or record of the 16th assembly session that we were looking at yesterday. It's still on page 13 of the English, which is page 7 of the Serbian. We already looked at the paragraph where Dr. Karadzic discusses the third strategic goal. And then the next paragraph he says, "The fourth strategic goal is establishment of the border on the Una and the Neretva rivers, on their working maps proposed at the last session, the European Community recognised the border on the Una. They marked the Una as our wartime border and painted everything east of it blue." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, there appears -- you've done marking on map B and exactly the same marking on map C, and apparently exactly the same marking on map D in relation to strategic objective 4, and I'm not sure whether you still have in front of you, Mr. Treanor's map. That's P68 tab 16. But it also appears, Mr. Krajisnik, that there is no material difference between your markings on all those maps and what Mr. Treanor has marked on his map. First of all, can you confirm that that's correct, Mr. Krajisnik? Mr. Treanor's marking goes further on, around the border. That's clear. But otherwise, so far as your marking is concerned, that coincides, doesn't it, with Mr. Treanor's marking for all practical purposes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is with regret that I have to say that Mr. Treanor's view is quite different from what our intentions were. And I can explain what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Please. We could take the objective -- I'm sorry, objective 4 is divided into two geographically separate points. Up in the northwest, the Una, and down in the south, the Neretva. Mr. Krajisnik we will take them in alphabetical order, shall we? You were looking at Neretva. Let's deal with that first.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Neretva River on this map. However, it is not being said here that the Neretva River should be the boundary but the valley of the Neretva River. You can take a look. I'm sure that that's what it says here. Sorry, just a moment, please. Well, I can't see now. The Una and Neretva rivers, yes, well, it says the Neretva River but it's really the Neretva River valley that is meant. Our only objective was this one here, near Mostar. That is where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik we will sort out later what to do about exhibit numbers. If you're going to say something like "this one here," I'm inviting you to -- if it's a point of any significance to mark what you mean by "here". Do you see? Otherwise it's not possible for anybody later to understand what your explanation has been. So whenever there is a significant point on the map for your explanation, perhaps you'd mark it in just the same way that you did a few minutes ago the other map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the only reference Mr. Krajisnik made to the map is he said this is the Neretva River here. I don't think even without any further marking, and also in view of the testimony that followed, that it should be rather the valley than the river itself, that it's clear enough on -- at least Mr. Treanor's map, and I think we are looking to Mr. Treanor's map at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two comments, if I may, Your Honour. First of all I was trying to led off the problem before it arose so we didn't have to go over anything twice and also, Your Honour, I must say with respect, I don't entirely share Your Honour's confidence in relation to page 21, line 7 and 8 where Mr. Krajisnik said "our only objective was this one here near Mostar." We can all identify where "near Mostar" is but that does seem to be a reference to a specific point on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Invite Mr. Krajisnik to make any markings you would like him to make though we might need a clear copy because this map has been admitted into evidence as it is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to give -- I can't give him mine because I've marked mine. It would obviously if that is the actual original exhibit, it would be better. I think we are given assistance such as we are often given and greatly appreciated by the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I make a suggestion? If you see any need of marking just ask-- invite Mr. Krajisnik and just tell him could you please mark Mostar with a 1 or 2? That's ten words. I'm quite sure Mr. Krajisnik will do it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked it over there on that map, and on this one that you have before you. I marked the Neretva River valley area. That is the strategic objective, not the entire current of the Neretva River but exactly where Mostar is. The Neretva River valley where Mostar is. I can show that, but you have this marked exactly. It's perhaps 10 or 15 kilometres. We were interested in that because you can see on this blue-green --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're referring, I take it to the D192D, the most southerly small parallel lines going approximately north-south, almost at the bottom? Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think B and C, Your Honour, where there is a clear red line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On C there is the small red line with -- could I say -- which is the starting point for the black arrow going in southwesterly direction, the middle of the 3 on that map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, was it -- well, that's Neretva. Let's just look at the other part of objective 4 first, the Una River up in the northwest.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you -- your again B and C, you have marked not along the borders but running from the border to the southwest, to the border on the northeast. Do you wish to add any explanation in relation to that which is marked on maps B, C, and D?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we have Mr. Treanor's map, this is the Una River. Now, I have to mark this here. From here to the very end is the border with Croatia, with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik, could you mark with a number 1 -- Mr. Krajisnik, when you say here and you point to the map, would you mark that with a number, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. From here, from this part, to this other part here, so this is 1. This is 2. That is the riverbed itself, or rather 3. That is the river that's the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. From 1 up to 4 over here is the boundary within Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is the Una River as a strategic objective within Bosnia-Herzegovina. From 4 up to 5, there is also a boundary between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. Our strategic goal is only part of the Una River here, number 6, which separated Muslim and Serb parts within Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I drew on these maps. We were not interested now in borders with Croatia. So this is what was drawn on the Cutileiro plan. Take a look and you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, I do notice that by comparing the maps, it looks as if Mr. Treanor's line just west of -- you see where your number 6, your black line, goes down and joins the blue line, you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You mean Mr. Treanor, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Just to the west -- if we go to where that black line joins the blue line, if we go to the west, it looks as if Mr. Treanor's line does go out noticeably further to the west there than your red lines on maps B, C and D. First of all, do you agree and is that quite deliberate, so far as your line marking is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deliberately do this. It's very clear that this is the Una River, and possibly this was a mistake, well, since I don't have the actual Una River here, perhaps I made a mistake to the left or to the right. Mr. Treanor, Mr. Cutileiro and I bore in mind the fact that the Una River was the strategic objective. Now, since I did not have the map here, rather I didn't have the river on the map here, that's why I drew it the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it sounds to me as if possibly whatever word you got in Serbian from my word deliberately was understood to imply something negative. The English word wasn't. It -- yes. Well, you've -- thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't think it was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well in that case, it's a non-issue, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it was a mistake. Possibly it was a mistake. Yes. But it was the Una River that was the border in all of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, as far as the -- these strategic goals go, where did you see strategic goal 4 in difficulty or comparative ease in achieving and agreeing that goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we talked to the Croatian side, and we did not find a satisfactory solution for the Neretva River valley, for the Neretva have to be the boundary. They wanted Marshal Tito street to be the boundary. They wanted the entire town to be theirs. That was what they wanted. When we had these preliminary talks before the assembly, we just wanted the Una to be a strategic objective because it was envisaged by the Cutileiro plan. However, there was a big group of MPs from Herzegovina who in a way brought pressure to bear, namely that the Neretva River area should be included, although I must say quite frankly that this was not an objective or goal because the Croatian side was strongly opposed to it and we knew that there was an interest involved on the Muslim side as well. In a way -- I'm sorry, I am sorry. Well, it doesn't matter now. Somewhere around Stolac. They wanted that area to be annexed to some entity of theirs. The Cutileiro map did not envisage any part of the Neretva River valley to belong to us. So I know that this was pressure but we thought that we could come through as far as the Una River was concerned because that was clearly the position of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then, going back to the minute or record of the assembly session, page 13 of the English, page 7 in your document, foot of page 13 of the English, the fifth strategic goal is division of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts, and implementation of an effective state government in each of those two constituent states. Thus, "Sarajevo is strategically in the fifth place but the battle in Sarajevo and for Sarajevo, seen strategically and tactically, is of decisive importance because it does not allow the establishment of even the illusion of a state. Alija does not have a state while we have a part of Sarajevo." Mr. Krajisnik, could you explain why Dr. Karadzic is saying that Sarajevo is of decisive importance because it does not allow the establishment of even the illusion of a state for, clearly, the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that was a strategic objective was the first sentence, that after -- well, how should I put this? After the United Nations we would have part of Sarajevo. That was in the Cutileiro plan as well. It was looked into. And then we left it under UN supervision and then we would find a solution for Sarajevo subsequently. Now, what was Mr. Karadzic explaining here? He is speaking in Banja Luka. I've already explained that in socialism there was this animosity from Banja Luka vis-a-vis Sarajevo, and it was quite justified. This refers to the former system. I am from Sarajevo but I'm telling you the way it was. All resources were concentrated in Sarajevo. Banja Luka was sinking lower and lower, and in terms of development, it fell to the 22nd place in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All people from Krajina continued thinking that way too, that we would continue this policy of focusing on Sarajevo, and that is why Mr. Karadzic is explaining why Sarajevo is important for us. Well, he didn't do it here but he was saying how the Jews and the Palestinians were fighting for Jerusalem because that is the capital of a state. Now, what he said later as an additional argument, since Sarajevo was the capital city, and for as long as we have part of Sarajevo, for as long as we have the right to part of Sarajevo, it is not only the Muslim side that is the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are not the only ones who have a state. Let's put it this way. We are the state because a capital city is always referred to and whoever has the capital city is portrayed in the media as governing a state. What he was saying in particular was that in Sarajevo, there was a large concentration of population and, of course, of the military too, of the Muslim army. And now he's saying, if we did not have our own territories then those armed forces would have a lot more manoeuvring space, the Muslim armed forces would, and that would bring pressure on the Krajina. All of that is by way of propaganda because people, our MPs, did not understand and they didn't wish to understand the importance of Sarajevo. As I've already said, in the former Yugoslavia, Sarajevo was the second largest Serb city and we didn't want to be excommunicated from Sarajevo. We wanted to have at least those rural areas if we could not have part of urban Sarajevo. And this was agreed upon in a preliminary manner and in all the maps, Your Honours, in all the maps, excluding Pale, which is separate, I haven't got the map here, Pale is totally to the east, and there is this big territory. In all maps, what was envisaged was that one-third of this remainder of Sarajevo, excluding Pale, should belong to the Serbs and two-thirds to the Muslim-Croat federation or rather the Muslim side because they were interested. Not a division. I repeat that once again. In every case, we wanted it to be like Washington DC and I don't know what else. Everybody kept saying that this would be a separate entity that would have a council of its own but in these different neighbourhoods there could be local laws and perhaps there could even be some emblems of the constituent units but economically and politically, this would be united at city level. I have a paper here where agreement was supposed to be reached on Sarajevo even before Dayton and in Dayton, and indeed this kind of solution was agreed upon in Dayton, that Sarajevo should not be divided. And then it was changed and Sarajevo was divided. I can give you documents for everything I'm saying. Please, if ever there is any dilemma, I'm going to get the right document and I'm going to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- you say, specifically in that answer, you say -- this is line -- page 28 for everybody's else's reference in the transcript, 28, line 6, you say, "in all maps what was envisaged was that one-third of this remainder of Sarajevo excluding Pale should belong to the Serbs and two-thirds to the Muslim-Croat federation or, rather, the Muslim side because they were interested. Not a division. I repeat that once again." So how was -- how were Dr. Karadzic's words understood in Banja Luka in May 1992 when he introduced the fifth strategic goal by saying the fifth strategic goal is division of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: An atmosphere of war. I remember that assembly. Everybody was thinking in his own way, in his own head. Everybody was just looking at their local problems, if I can put it that way. Somebody was just thinking of the corridor, somebody of the other corridor, somebody else, access to the sea and so on and so forth. I assure you that this strategic objective was something that perhaps ten per cent of the MPs were interested in because, quite simply, they weren't paying any attention. I believe that there were different ways of understanding this because there were quite a few MPs, you will see the discussion later, who thought we shouldn't live together any longer. We should have a division, because they didn't want to observe this and so on and so forth. Probably that group thought that now Sarajevo would be divided. But I assure you that everything Mr. Karadzic is saying here is based on what we advocated in the negotiations and what we will advocate in the negotiations if we adopt this appeal to continue the conference. That was our objective. You will see, Your Honours, that the MPs were saying all sorts of things. Quite simply everybody spoke in his own way and we were just trying to explain to them what it was that we were discussing at the negotiations because before that there were negotiations in Brussels and they were interested in seeing whether anybody had committed any kind of betrayal, what was to be done with which territory and so on. And in their own heads, some of them were thinking there will be no negotiations. There will just be war. I don't preclude that possibility either, but I assure you that this entire session had one single goal. For us to explain what we were advocating, politically, and to try to continue the conference. And many thought that it was unnecessary, that there would be no conference whatsoever, because we had been betrayed, we had been cheated. There was no transformation of Bosnia, and Bosnia had been recognised nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm coming to the 6th strategic objective. If Your Honour wants me to the sea before 10.30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how much time you would need for the sixth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not long but more than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do it within five minutes you may continue, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is a pretty good chance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then try to do it in five minutes then we will have a break until 11 afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, strategic objective 6, the 6th strategic goal, I will in the interests of time on this, I won't then read out the longish paragraph in Dr. Karadzic's speech. It is -- it's relatively straightforward and you'll be familiar with it. What I'm going to invite you to do, Mr. Krajisnik, is if you could just give a brief explanation of your red lines which are the same on the various maps, B, C, and D. Mr. Treanor didn't attempt any lines there. He just gives a big, black arrow pointing into the sea. Could you -- you've got the two lines, the one going diagonally, and then there are two little lines together just to the southeast of that. I wonder if you could offer the Trial Chamber an explanation of what you have marked on these maps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I put this map on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would no doubt be very helpful, Mr. Krajisnik, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This arrow here, number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we now marking another map because there is the one on which -- or is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A new map. Maybe we can do it on the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps take the other one. Otherwise we have such a huge, all the markings on the same map, not that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you could take map B in that little clip. I think the lines are the same on B and C?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. We used -- I said the marked map would be E, and that's the one I'd like to have further markings made on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Can Your Honour just remind me which that was drawn from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have a problem because I see that was already for the Una River markings were already on another map as well. Let's take the clear map. Then we have -- I -- I didn't notice that, that we have now the -- well, let's say the Posavina markings on number E. We would then have the Una River markings should then be F, because that's another map from what I -- oh, yes, no. That was marked on -- yes. We can use E again because the markings on the Una River were made on a new copy of the P68, well, let's say the Treanor map. Okay. Please proceed on number E. That is the already-marked map. Yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could we just move that on so that we can see the south access to the sea? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since Bosnia and Herzegovina is clearly marked on this map, you see, the outlet to the sea would be here. I'll mark it now with 7, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That seems to make sense, Mr. Krajisnik, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in the area of Prevlaka, Molunat and Prevlaka, the Serb side would have access to the sea. In exchange, we would give the hinterland of Dubrovnik to the Croat side. That's number 8, this blue area here, and that would be a swap of territories. That was indeed agreed in Dayton and the proposal was made, but they forgot to sign it. Let me now tell you why we thought we were entitled to this. The Cutileiro plan did not offer us this. This is number 9. This here is the Bosnian access to the sea. And on account of the entitlement of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we demanded that we too have access to the sea, rather than the Croat community only. I have this plan discussed in Dayton for the exchange of territories, and according to the Stoltenberg plan, it was also envisaged. Croatia gave its agreement, Bosnia and Herzegovina gave its agreement, and Yugoslavia too. That was a most serious proposal. We suggested that the Muslim side have access too, in an exchange for Neum. However the Croats didn't agree with this because it would cut their territory into two. The Muslims didn't ask for it any way. Only we asked in the negotiations for access to the sea. That's something that was discussed in Graz and even previously with the Croat side, and I have to tell you exactly what I heard from Mr. Tudjman personally. He said, "I understand the Serb side in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a stone's throw from their territory to the sea and still they don't have access to it." And indeed, this proposal was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Your Honour, may I just very simply -- before the break, might I inquire if Your Honours could let us know, not right now but conveniently soon, where we, the Defence, have got to in terms of the timing of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence? We had that late start the first day and then, of course, there may have been other matters. I'm wondering because Your Honour has the computer information. I'm wondering if we could be informed where we have got to so that we can finalise our planning of bringing Mr. Krajisnik's evidence to a conclusion in a helpful, planned way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter and let you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, please proceed. Mr. Josse it's you who is going to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is I. I'm going to be on my feet for a little time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same to the Bench. The Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Court, my learned friends, and indeed Mr. Krajisnik's information, I'm going to go through some further intercepts during the course of this morning. Probably tomorrow, I will then invite Mr. Krajisnik to comment specifically on certain allegations that have been made in the course of the Prosecution case by various Prosecution witnesses. That's the plan, at least, Your Honour. There is in existence a further bundle of intercepts that have been prepared, all the remaining intercept that I'm going to invite Mr. Krajisnik to deal with have previously been exhibited, Your Honour. As Your Honour is aware, Mr. Krajisnik has his own version of these. I gave them to him with the Court's permission last week and I see he's got them open in front of him. Could the remaining bundles be handed out? They've already been given to the interpreters. There is a large bundle with a much smaller additional bundle of one particular intercept which I left out of the original group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber, for logistical reasons, would not mind if we find them on our desk when coming into the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I take responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we are first going to look at an intercept between you and Mr. Tintor. It is dated the 3rd of April of 1992. It doesn't actually say that on the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the third page of the first intercept in the bundle. The others -- these were exhibited as a group. The others don't involve Mr. Krajisnik and I'm not going to ask him about them. This is simply one page long, at least in the English, and as I understand it's P529, tab 377. It was mentioned in passing, I understand, during the evidence of Ms. Hanson but only in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see that you say to Mr. Tintor, "War must not be provoked no matter what. If he" -- maybe a translation issue here -- "or they wants to get in, let him or they get in but please take no war." Answer: "No problem." You go on: "Take my advice. The people are, God forbid, that somebody gets killed. Everything will be a problem. Please, we should not be the ones to start. We simply have to do what we are entitled to do and what we are not we shall not do it. Isn't that so?" Tintor: "Certainly." You go on: "I am asking you to listen to me and discuss with the Rajko as well, calmly and slowly, no matter what comes, because as long as there is no war, nothing is lost. Is that okay?" Later on, very near the end of the intercept, you say, "Avoid everything in order to prevent the war, sit down and talk with them, agree about it." Answer: "Certainly." And then you say: "If there is a need for shooting, we should talk first. Don't do it, please." "All right, certainly no problem." And then you say, "Do not let the war to start." What's this about, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which intercept that is? Because I've read it but it's not arranged in sequence here so I can't find it. I remember reading that intercept. The first one I have is 388, written in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is that the B/C/S is in manuscript for some strange reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's the one which we find in the bundle -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Krajisnik, it says 6 in handwriting at the top of the page, top of page 6 in your version.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Are there two other manuscripts coming before it, also in manuscript? This one ends in -- the ERN number ends in 481.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They don't involve you and I'm not asking any questions about the two that come before this one. You heard me read various extracts [Microphone not activated] You are clearly telling Mr. Tintor that war should not break out. What is going on at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I don't remember this particular intercept this minute but I remember the circumstances he was very highly strung, frightened, and I had several conversations with him in the same vein, when he called me to get some more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at I think the next one which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is another one between the same two protagonists, not the next one in the bundle, in fact, I'm going to leave that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is the following day, the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's quite short. Mr. Tintor says to you, the middle of the intercept: "Look I called you this morning to check about this thing. These people from slow and ski Brod have been calling me. Fuck, military." You say: "Look, Simovic and Doko have gone there. I called down there. The SDS and HDZ representatives, they will receive them, go there and try to calm the situation down. I know that this vice-president of theirs from the HDZ, what's his name?" What's that about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an MP there, Mr. Stanic. He is mentioned in one assembly session transcript as captured by the Muslim forces, and I intervened -- by the Serb side, and I intervened through Trifko Radic that he be released. I called this Mr. Stanic here. He is mentioned as being the president of HDZ. Simovic and Doko went to see him. That was Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is said that they had gone there and would talk to the parties. That was the first contact between Bosanski Brod and Slavonski Brod to solve some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This intercept was referred to on the 12th of April 2005, when Mr. Kljuic, it appears, was asked some questions by Judge Orie, and Mr. Kljuic said that the intercept explains the situation in Bosanski Brod and the bridge which could no longer be used by that time. Anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You have this previous intercept when a different delegation had travelled, Mr. Ejup Ganic and Mr. Koljevic, and it was my conversation with Mr. Koljevic, saying that two delegations went to try to resolve this problem of the bridge between Bosanski Brod and Slavonski Brod across the Sava River, and Mr. Kljuic is right, the problem was that this bridge was closed down and citizens on both sides really needed to use it. There was also the surrounding crisis and the high tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we now turn, not to the next intercept? I'm going to come back to that in a moment but the one after that because that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recollection, although I'm looking quickly through the transcript is that this second intercept, although there was a reference to its appearance in testimony on a particular date, was not referred to by any previous number or was not given a number. I don't recall off-hand whether the first intercept was referred to by a pre-existing exhibit number or received a new number. But if we are going to be going through intercepts I think we should be identifying them as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I agree with that. I do not know whether they have a specific number. I'm told by the person who assisted me with this that it's part of P292. That is all I know, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The additional information I have is that it is P292, KID, 31143.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Up until this point we have not given additional exhibit numbers to those intercepts that I've asked Mr. Krajisnik about, D-numbers. We could start doing that now but we probably should have done -- started that two weeks ago but I'm entirely neutral about this, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have to think it over, whether we need -- I mean, if we haven't done it for the last two weeks, it can wait for one more day. And perhaps I should -- first of all it should be clear that whenever we are talking about intercepts that they should be clearly identified which ones they are. I'll try to sort this out with Mr. Registrar, and come up with a solution most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if this will be of assistance, it appears that we -- looking at the list provided by the Defence, we have exhibit numbers, specific exhibit numbers, for all of the intercepts contained in the bundle. In that connection I would mention that the first intercept referred to today appears to have been P529, tab 377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I checked that and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I knew that and I put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. For the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I have an extra copy of that so maybe it would be useful for Mr. Josse as he goes through the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he can refer to it and I'll try to get them on my screen so there -- can verify whether we are -- no, no, to Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to my learned friends. As I think everyone is aware, the tab number on the left-hand side of this index is a Defence working system, so to speak, which no one else in this courtroom need worry about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could turn next to -- I will use those numbers simply because that's probably going to be the easiest way for people to identify where I'm going -- to 178, which is P529, tab 406. This is another intercept on the same day between the same two gentlemen. Mr. Krajisnik, I assume that this is later in the day because this one begins with a "good evening." The one we have just looked at begins with a "good afternoon." I want to take you to the middle of this particular page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Tintor says, "I hear you've been informed, Rajko has told me about that part. They are getting ready up there. Reportedly they are on the move already." Krajisnik: "Who is on the move?" Tintor: "Well, the Muslims from Kobilja Glava." Krajisnik: "Yeah." Tintor: "They are on their way towards Grahoviste, towards Zuc and the situation is tense. I think a conflict will break out up there." What's that about, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the line was established between two warring parties in Vogosca, a significant part of Vogosca ended up in Muslim hands. A part that is not in the urban area of Vogosca, it's called Kobilja Glava. And now Mr. Tintor reports that the Muslims set out from Kobilja Glava, from Sarajevo, from the east, towards them, towards Vogosca, and they want to take control of this settlement Grahoviste and another one, Zuc. I had my doubts about this but the basic point is that the Muslims did indeed go for Grahoviste and captured a certain number of civilians whom they took to Sarajevo. I'll remind you that the president of Vogosca municipality testified here, saying that in agreement with the Serb side, he later went to Sarajevo to find those six Serbs, but he couldn't find out from the Presidency in which prison they were detained because there were many prisons among them, private prisons, and their corpses were subsequently found. However, they didn't attack Vogosca. They attacked this place Grahoviste instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turning the page in the English -- sorry, question: The Rajko being referred to in both these intercepts is whom, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Rajko Kopravica, president of the executive council of Vogosca municipality, the local government, from before the armed conflict. It's the highest position on the Serb side in the Vogosca municipality, joint, as it were. And later he was also at the head of the local government during the armed conflict. He died recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I mentioned, over the page in the English, you say, "I told him to inform this Momo Mandic for the police, you know." And then a few lines after that, you go on, "That's the most important thing. Finally, the people do need to organise themselves but in no circumstances should we look for trouble. It's very important to keep peace, you know." Now, this intercept, Mr. Krajisnik, was played in this Court on the 2nd of March of 2005, at page 9774 in the transcript, during the evidence of Ms. Hanson, and she suggested that this intercept shows that you were being informed about the situation on the ground, bearing in mind that Mr. Tintor was apparently the president of the Vogosca Crisis Staff. What do you say about Ms. Hanson's assertion in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct, but I'll explain what this is about, and I understand how she got confused, how she got the wrong impression. This place is the next to my municipality, next door to my village. We call each other neighbour normally, even though we are at a distance of one or two kilometres because we all attended the same primary school. I knew personally both Mr. Rajko Kopravica and Mr. Tintor and I can understand -- I can explain why he calls me "kum," best man. Beset by misfortune and panic, they are in -- addressing me looking for help, expecting me to find a way to help them. It's not somebody who was 500 kilometres away but somebody closer by. He called me and Mr. Tintor called me too, Mr. Rajko Kopravica and Mr. Tintor. In our part of the world, if you know somebody who holds some position, you call him even though it's not strictly within his area of competence, asking him to find somebody who could possibly help them. Gentlemen prosecutors and Your Honours, you remember when the problem of the police was discussed, when the police station was divided, when they quarrelled amongst themselves and even a protected witness explained how no agreement could be reached about the police. He mentioned this problem of the police and I said, "Call Mr. Mandic to deal with it because he knows Mandic no better, no worse, than he knows me." That is the point of this conversation. And since Mrs. Hanson is not aware of these mutual relations, she, with good reason, tried to explain it in her own way, concerning the issue to what extent somebody at the top was informed. She used this to illustrate. It would have been different if somebody from Sanski Most had called me. I was practically a local of this area and an MP for this constituency. It has nothing to do with me personally but I couldn't say "No, I don't want to talk to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next conversation? This is one several weeks later, on the 21st of April, between you and someone called Momo Garic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is P67, tab 29, and P529, tab 407. And I will put it in the context of the evidence in a few moments' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Garic, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way I verified both numbers and they are both correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, who is Mr. Garic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Garic is a man from Vraca, that is to say from Novo Sarajevo, whom I knew. It's also mentioned in this material when I once asked him to send a fax or something like that. I knew him personally and I tried to receive information from him because he lived there. He lived in Sarajevo, at Vraca. That's to say on this hill above Grbavica. He's an acquaintance of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The conversation begins with someone from your office trying to get through to him. That person succeeds and on the second page in the English, we see the substance of the conversation. You ask what the situation is like. Mr. Garic says, "Well, there are some little problems. Could you receive me up there for a brief meeting?" Answer: "Well, sure, no problem." Couple of lines down; "All right, I'll come there, I'll find some vehicle, I'll come there." And you ask, "What the situation like up there?" And Mr. Garic says, "Well, it's all right for the time being, we had some casualties and many wounded." Now, this has been played twice to this Court, once on the 26th of February of 2004, at page 1695 of the transcript, during the course of Mr. Treanor's evidence. He says that it is significant because it shows that you at that point, president of the assembly but also a member of the National Security Council was dealing directly with a Territorial Defence commander on the local military situation in that commander's area. It was also played on the 2nd of March of 2005, at page 9776, in the course of Ms. Hanson's evidence. She said that this showed you were informed about the situation on the ground because of Mr. Garic's membership of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. So two similar points by the two experts brought before this Chamber by the Prosecution. What do you say about their assertions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point they were advocating, that they were trying to justify, was actually done without going into detail. I am from Sarajevo. I was personally interested in what the situation was like in every single part of Sarajevo. This is a private, a personal matter, not only because I'm an MP. And, I didn't call colonels, generals, and I don't know who else, I called people I knew. So that they would tell me about it, just like any person would express this kind of interest. In terms of his broader neighbourhood, if I can put it that way. It is not put in any other way at all. It's not that I'm saying, now, you report to me and so on and so forth. No. You just hear some information. What is going on where you are? You don't know what this is all about. You don't know whether a friend got killed, whether there is someone who is doing something on his own. I am personally interested, because independently from one's high office, one has personal reasons for being interested in the place that he's from. So now I'm asking him, if you remember, Your Honours, there was this conversation that was played here between me and Karisik, Milenko Karisik, this policeman I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... say that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are literally going to play that in one moment.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right. I just wanted to say one thing and I'll finish. I'm so sorry, I do apologise. You're quite right. I just wanted to say the following. My communication with these people was on a personal basis. I was talking to people I knew. I did not call on the basis of the high office I held. I didn't call any commander saying now you report to me and whatever. I will remind you that this is the third day since I got to Pale. Or was it the fourth day? I came on the 15th. On the 15th of April. And then I returned to Zabrdje and then I went back to Pale. I assume it was the first or the second day. Or the third day. I don't know. I can't be very accurate on that. If you remember, that meeting of the national security council on the 15th, it was stated that I was present there and that I returned to Zabrdje, and then again with my family I came to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the conversation that you were just referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is found, the next tab. It's also, in fact, the tab after that, 180 and 181 in our presentation are identical. They bear completely different ERN numbers, however, but we think that the translations are the same. There are therefore three relevant -- I beg your pardon, two relevant exhibit numbers, P67, tab 30 and P292, KID, 31205.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any tab number on the 529?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is no 529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought you just said -- let me just check. You said P292, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a conversation that involves Radomir Ninkovic, Milenko Karisik, Nikola Koljevic at one point, and yourself, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm only going to refer to one short passage. Towards the bottom of the second page in the English, Karisik says, "Well, we know everything. We know everything. We know everything. The forces of the Serb ministry are not engaged but they are shooting at us here. They shot at us from hand-held rocket launchers. Most missed but one projectile hit the F facility where we are." Krajisnik: "Yes." Karisik: "Was supposed to enter in our base. Three walls have been penetrated. They shot at us from snipers and things like that. However, we have stayed here and we are calm. We returned a couple of rounds, just what we had to and nothing more." Krajisnik: "Yes, yes." Karisik: "It's mainly members of the TO who are engaged. As far as I know the army hasn't shot at all." Krajisnik: "Yes, yes. It's chaos. And the army can't engage because then we would have real problems. Can you make contact with them just so that we know how they are doing?
