I need to know this, damn it." What did you mean when you said "real problems"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read the entire conversation, as far as this same locality is concerned, Vraca, there was a need to talk to the police, because Mr. Koljevic expected a delegation of the European Community. So I talked to this Mr. Karisik now, whom I also know, and I had a conversation that was similar to the one I had had with Garic. Until Mr. Koljevic got involved too, in order to ask the basic question, namely whether the delegation of the European Community had arrived. The essence of this is that he is saying that it was the armed people, not the army, not the police. I would like to remind you and the Honourable Trial Chamber that that is when a cease-fire was being sought, and Mrs. Plavsic talked to Mr. Stanisic. She was still in Muslim Sarajevo. There were a lot of mutual accusations that were leveled, but it was necessary to establish a cease-fire and it was necessary to continue talks on the problems in Ilidza, if I remember correctly. So I took advantage of this opportunity to discuss this same subject with Karisik until Mr. Koljevic got involved too in order to deal with the main topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did Mrs. Plavsic ask of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic was in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, I've already said that, and she was with Mr. Doyle. And UNPROFOR was guarding her from these gangs that were out of control at the time. No one had control over them. They were on the Muslim side. If you remember, one particular document, she was in charge of contacts with UNPROFOR. This is one of the conclusions of this National Security Council, as we called it. So she was in contact with them and they said, well, try to get the Serb side to stop shooting and we will reach agreement with the Muslim side, to establish a cease-fire and to have problems resolved. In this conversation, she resolutely said to Mr. Stanisic, the MUP minister who was there and she sought information about what was going on, you ever the conversation here and I have the conversation here, and she said, "You have to observe this. I order you to do that so that we should not be blamed, even if they shoot at you, let us just resolve this problem." It's easy to find this conversation and to see that it is in the framework of everything that was going on. Now, three days later, Mr. Karisik says, we are not responding, the army is not involved. Now, look, they even destroyed the wall of the building that we are in and we only respond when absolutely forced to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When this intercept was played in the course of Mr. Treanor's evidence, at page 1695 of the transcript, he made a similar point, the point he had made so far as the previous intercept is concerned, and he says that this shows that you were dealing with a prominent police commander trying to get information about the situation in Sarajevo. What did you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope -- well, it's fully understandable that Mr. Treanor came to that conclusion, although he came to the wrong conclusion. I had been in Pale only for two or three days perhaps, and you saw that as far as coordination of the Territorial Defence is concerned, and National Defence, Mr. Karadzic was in charge of that. I had no role in this. But Mr. Treanor didn't know that, and Mrs. Hudson [as interpreted] didn't know it either. Actually I was just expressing my interest when I talked to people I knew. It had nothing to do with the office I held. So that I would receive information as a citizen who lived in Sarajevo and who had a personal interest involved. I was asking whether there was anything wrong, and I would try to intervene with those who were responsible to prevent that kind of thing from happening. Because I was interested in that as a private person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse could I just ask one question? A little bit further up in that same conversation, you ask, Mr. Krajisnik, "Do we know who initiated the whole thing?" And then Mr. Karisik answers: "Well, I don't know if I should talk about that on the phone now." And then you say, "No, don't, don't, but" -- and then the conversation continues. That suggests that who initiated the matter should not be known to others who may listen in. Could you explain two situations? If it was your side that had initiated, whether it would make sense not to discuss it on the phone, and the same question for -- if the other party would have initiated it, where it seems to be known, whether it would make sense not to discuss it on the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian language, when you listen to this intercept, I clearly indicated that I was concerned over the possibility that someone from the Serb side did it. I received that information, that somebody did something in adventurous fashion. Now, there was no dilemma there. Now, why did he have to say to me, Petar or whoever did that? I said, well, don't, because I knew that someone in an unauthorised adventurous manner, did something that was deadly and ill conceived. I didn't want that to happen. I certainly could have called Mr. Karadzic and I could have said, "Well, you're in charge of that. Could you please try to intervene so that these people would not do that?", although I don't think I could have done anything like that or actually I don't see what I could have done. For me, it was not in dispute, well, maybe it was in dispute, but that this was an individual or a group from the Serb side that did something that was impermissible. And it was mentioned here. I wasn't worried about whether the Muslim side did that. Why did the Serb side do that? This is the kind of information that got to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on, please, to a conversation on the 7th of May of 1992 between you and someone called Karlo. I think you referred to this conversation yesterday at page 13 of the transcript when you were talking about Territorial Defence in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We -- this is P627. We see on the second page in the English, that Karlo says, "And somewhere around the tobacco factory and onwards to Korija [phoen] the mall, they are shooting from there but only on and off. There would be a lot of fire for ten minutes and then everything goes quiet. So it's nothing really special. Well, nothing much, right? No. Who told me this? This Professor Plavsic." Karlo goes on, "Oh, yes, she's down there and hears the echoing and thinks it's where we were." Karlo says, "But we had two or three terrible nights. Then it stopped." First question, Mr. Krajisnik, is who is Karlo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karlo is one and the same person, Mr. Karisik. Well, it was sort of a nom de guerre. It's one and the same person, Mr. Milenko Karisik. I'm sorry, I noted something down here, that on the 14th of May, Mr. Stanisic talked to Mrs. Plavsic. That's the conversation I referred to a few moments ago. The 14th of May. I'm sure that the gentlemen of the Prosecution have this and I have it here in my records. So it's the 14th of May. On the 20th of May, she left town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then the second part of this conversation, Mr. Djeric takes over and continues speaking with Karlo. I'd like to move on, please, to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is something that's important here. Who said this? Professor Plavsic. Mrs. Plavsic called me from the Muslim part of Sarajevo because I was in Pale, and that is how come Karlo and I had this conversation and she was probably saying that something was going on at Grbavica. So that's why I'm talking to him. Afterwards, Mr. Djeric, the Prime Minister, takes the receiver from me. We were probably together. And then he talks to him. You can see here that she had informed me. And I remember that we had whatever, two or three conversations. She was in Sarajevo and I was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, would you allow me to go back briefly to one of my previous questions? Because otherwise it might slip out of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik if I understood you well when I asked you the question about who might have initiated that -- attack or at least that shooting, did I then understand well that you -- the one who called you, I think it was in Vraca, that you thought it to be possible that Serb shooting was directed against other Serbs at this moment, when you said it was an irresponsible act? Is that how I have to understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received information from someone that the Serb side took some action, not against the Serbs, but probably against the Muslims. It was excessive. I don't know whether it's correct, but I assumed and I was worried. Why was this done? There was a cease-fire of sorts. That is why I had already formed an opinion that the Serb side had done something that was wrong and that's why I raised the issue with him. So it was against the Muslims, not against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Karisik says, "But they are shooting at us here. They shot at us from hand-held rocket launchers." Was that a response to what you called an irresponsible act by the Serbs? How do I have -- I'm just trying to get a picture of what happened at that time, because the earlier question was about who initiated that but at the same time, Mr. Karisik says that they are shooting at us from hand held rocket launchers. That was Muslims who would shoot at where Mr. Karisik was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these are two different cases. That was on the 21st of April, and this is the 7th of May. Now, when I talked about the first case, I was saying that somebody had acted in an adventure us fashion. That's the information that I received. As for the 7th of May, this was this contact between Mrs. Plavsic and UNPROFOR, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to limit the question entirely to the 21st of April. You said adventurous action taken by Serbs. That's the information you received. Now, this shooting at the place where Mr. Milenko Karisik was located, was that in return to that adventurous activity? Because he says, "They are shooting at us."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Throughout that time, there were mutual exchanges of gunfire. Now, what Mr. Karisik is saying here is that there had been an intention to impose a cease-fire, and somebody instructed them not even to respond with gunfire even when they are attacked by the Muslims from Vraca. He is just saying, we are just defending ourselves and we respond only when absolutely necessary, although they are shelling us, and this is the 7th of May when we are getting ready to go to Nevesinje. So these are two incidents, what we have before us now, and that is what Karisik is explaining, that the school that they are staying at is being shelled all the time. That is to say, that he is blaming the Muslim side, and they are not being allowed to respond. That's the way it was. And the first one was a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would be the case, I would have expected, as an answer, to do we know who initiated the whole thing to say, well, the Muslims because they started shelling us. That's initiating, unless it's a wrong understanding of the English or perhaps of the translation, who started -- who took the initiative? And I have some difficulties in reconciling that because there would hardly be any reason not to say that it was the Muslims who violated whatever cease-fire there was or -- and that they initiated it, therefore, and I do see later that a few rounds were fired in return. But it's -- it's still a puzzle for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would just have a little patience, I would try to be as precise as I can. This is the 7th of May. From the 4th of April until the 7th of May, and onwards, at the school building in Vraca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, Mr. Krajisnik. I am talking about a telephone conversation intercept that took place on the 21st of April so what happened on the 7th of May could not have influenced this conversation. I don't think I was clear enough when I said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come back to that conversation. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I would like you to concentrate on that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about Karisik, Koljevic, and -- that one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and especially the beginning before Mr. Koljevic enters the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's where I said, why not talk about who initiated the whole thing. That was my previous question to you. And then you said you -- you thought that it was possible that it was adventurous action by Serbs or by a Serb, and then I said but Mr. Karisik is talking about being fired at where he is located, and therefore I wondered whether that was a -- considered to be a Muslim response to the adventurous act or whether it was Serbs shooting at another Serb position. That's what I was trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We are only talking about the 21st of April, when I had two conversations with Garic and Mr. Karisik. And now we are discussing only the conversation with Karisik. Your Honours, throughout the time from the 4th of April until the 21st of April, at the school house in Vraca, the police was deployed, and that school was constantly shelled by the Muslim side. So that is not in dispute. And we wanted a cease-fire to start. However, according to the information provided by the UNPROFOR, they responded against the Muslims and one could no longer tell who is shelling whom and who is responding to whom. But our main objective to stop the shelling at all costs and that's the same thing that I mentioned with reference to Mrs. Plavsic. Now, speaking of Mr. Karisik, he is talking about what I called an adventurous, reckless action, the people in Vraca were constantly under fire and somebody made a recollection, adventurous move, taking proactive action against the Muslims. They probably set off downhill. It's not just that they were returning fire from the school building. Somebody must have said, "Let's take action now. Let's get involved." And at that time, even the EC monitors were supposed to come and verify that we were not shooting at them, that they were shooting at our men at Vraca, to have an objective assessment. That was our entire conversation. I received information that somebody on our side, on the Serb side, made an active move against the Muslims but you are right on one point, Your Honour. It came after a prolonged Muslim action against the police located in the school building. The Muslims simply wanted to drive them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the shooting with the hand-held rocket launchers was in response to that or was Mr. Karisik referring to any earlier event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you just indicate the passage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read that. Mr. -- after you discussed whether to discuss on the phone who initiated the whole thing, Mr. Karisik says, "Well, we know everything, we know everything, we know everything. The forces of the Serb ministry are not engaged but they are shooting at us here. They shot at us from hand-held rocket launchers. Most missed but one projectile hit the F facility where we are." And then he further describes what damage was done, adding that "they shot at us from snipers and things like that. However, we stayed here and we are calm. We returned a couple of rounds, just what we had to and nothing more."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Your Honour, that eloquently confirms what I just explained. It's not that the Serbs shot at them. The Serbs didn't shoot at the MUP. The Muslims shot from the other side. They even broke through the wall. He is talking about the other -- what the other side was doing. And what might have provoked somebody into an adventurous, reckless action, that was at the end of the day futile because it didn't succeed. And now he's talking about two things. Neither the JNA nor the MUP were involved in what I call this adventurous action, only the Territorial Defence. And when he's talking about the attack against them, the MUP, he's talking about the Muslims who were firing at that location from the other side of the Miljacka river from Sarajevo. I know exactly what this is about, and if you read the rest, you will understand that the monitors were expected at that moment to identify who was shooting at whom, and who was initiating all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to in fact take Mr. Krajisnik to an additional intercept, with -- dart around a little bit, but there are two other intercepts, one of which I have copies of, the others I don't, which shed some further light on the questions Your Honour has just been asking. The first was handed out in a loose-leaf bundle. Mr. Krajisnik doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik be provided with it? Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the other, perhaps I will try to organise during the break. If not, I'll simply tell the Trial Chamber the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Krajisnik, is P292, KID 39219. It's a conversation between you and someone called Milinkov [phoen]. And it's on the same day, the 21st of April. If we look towards the bottom of the page in the English, after some discussion of heavy shooting. You asked what part of the city this is. He says, "Grbavica 1 and Grbavica 2, all the way between Vrbanja bridge down the Miljacka to the Milutin Djuraskovic street near the Zeljeznicar stadium." And you ask: "And not over the Miljacka on the other side, right?" And he says: "No." He goes on and says, "They put up fierce resistance." I'm summarising now. He says, "We have around ten wounded, men, one killed so far." You asked for clarification of that and he tells you that someone called Zoran Josilo has been killed and you say, "My dear God." And you ask whether Mico is down there. Now, I in fact was going to ask you -- I wasn't going to deal with that in as much detail. I was going to ask you some questions about that in a few moments because Mr. Brown dealt with this in passing in the course of his evidence. But before I do that, bearing in mind the questions the learned judge has just asked you, does that shed any more light on the situation that you've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Milenkovic is a man I know. He was a secretary at the Crisis Staff. I wanted to find out from him -- I wasn't telling him, Why did you go and do that? I just wanted to get a picture of what was going on, and all this is about is this quote-unquote adventurous action that somebody irresponsibly started. I was finding out how many people were wounded, how many dead, because it was in my mind something very reckless, and I was calling people I knew to find out about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm asking this question for a reason. What is the precise name of this man Milinkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'll soon forget my own name, I'm afraid. I don't remember even his face any more, but I knew the man. He was a rank and file member of the SDS, an acquaintance. I met him at a meeting. He was a wonderful, very fine man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is Milinkovic his surname?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason I ask that, Your Honour, is that at page 16213 of the transcript, when Mr. Brown is asked about this intercept, it's transcribed as someone called "Milan Kovic," and that's why I wanted to clarify the matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll talk to the transcriber during the break. He's made the correction now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't check immediately but what you say is Mr. Brown must have, although he gave a different name, must have referred to Mr. Milinkovic is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, this transcript -- I beg your pardon, this intercept was referred to and the name of Milinkovic was wrongly transcribed as "Milan Kovic." There caused me some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you take it that this was a transcribing problem rather than that Mr. Brown was referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do because he definitely talks about KID 39219, so it's clearly this intercept. I'm going to deal in a moment with what Mr. Brown said about this intercept. I'd like to deal with that in conjunction with R187, which is some six weeks or so later. I'm going to go -- I'm going to dart around, Your Honour, for reasons I think will be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we later come to Mr. Brown's testimony, do you by any chance have the date as well or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I -- I -- could Your Honour give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise I'll find it, if you read the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I don't off-hand, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, tab 187 is a conversation between you and Radivoje Grkovic on the 27th of May of 1992. It is P292, KID 31425, and P389, KID 31425. Mr. Grkovic introduces himself at the beginning of the intercept as a battalion commander. And turning halfway through this quite long conversation, he answers a question -- you ask him about -- you say, "So no one is attacking the barracks?" He says: "We have no information, President. No one is attacking it now." They seized the convoy, was broken down during the evacuation towards Ilidza, towards Lukavica, actually, it was going in several directions. The convoy was broken. The action wasn't coordinated. It wasn't -- it was coordinated by an idiot from Belgrade. Boskovic betrayed it, you know. You say: "You know what I'm interested in." Question: "What, president?" Answer: "A lot of equipment was left there. Cannons, howitzers, and things." Grkovic: "Believe me, I don't know anything about it but I'm in touch with" -- Krajisnik: "And do any of your men know?" Grkovic: "I really don't know. I suppose the men in Lukavica don't know." Well, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, what's this about, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the topic has already been discussed but I'll repeat. The evacuation of barracks from Sarajevo was agreed with the Muslim side. The Yugoslav People's Army and the Muslim side and on several occasions representatives of the JNA came from Belgrade. What I mean is among them was the then-assistant for security, Mr. Boskovic. And that evacuation followed after the massacre that happened when this column of troops was leaving Sarajevo. The command of the 2nd Military District. Let me mention one more thing. Instead of Kukanjac, it was Mr. Mladic who led this operation on behalf of those units of the Yugoslav People's Army who were there. Since Mr. Boskovic had come from Belgrade, they had various contacts with the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was Mr. Abdic who was their contact person in the Presidency, and an agreement was signed for them to be given safe passage. I don't know the exact terms of that agreement. I heard that evening -- somebody called me to tell me, because it was also in the area where I lived. Somebody called to tell me that the barracks was under attack and that area also held some civilians. So I made this call to find out more and this Grkovic person, whom I didn't know, picked up the receiver and he told me the barracks are no longer attacked. They have been evacuated already. But this column is under attack, and we don't know who is dead and who is alive. I'm paraphrasing now. Maybe the agreement was different. I'm certain that this action was led by Mr. Boskovic representing Belgrade and Mr. Mladic representing the JNA in Sarajevo. And we were an interested party, a concerned party, because there was a lot of weaponry in those barracks, according to our semi-reliable information, and I wanted to find out if the report we got was correct, that the barracks were under attack or whether the agreement had been observed. You remember this document we had here, the book of Karim Loncarevic, The Battle for Sarajevo. He wrote about how much weaponry was seized and how many weapons they saw at the barracks of Josip Broz Tito. This Mr. Loncarevic and the others did not honour the agreement with the JNA. Instead, they seized a lot of weapons from the barracks, in violation of the agreement. And I have to say that the soldiers we interviewed denied that that amount of weaponry had been left behind. And we were not sure whether they were lying because they didn't want to be held responsible for leaving so much weaponry behind, or there was something else to it. But we never managed to find out exactly which information is correct, the one we were given by the officers or what Mr. Loncarevic wrote. I just wanted to find out about it because I was interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, so far as this conversation was concerned, and the one that we have just looked at on the 21st of April, between you and Mr. Milinkovic, Mr. Brown commented in relation to both, that it would appear that you, Mr. Krajisnik, had an ability to speak to low-level commanders in order to avail yourself of the situation in the territory. What do you say about Mr. Brown's conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were present heard who was in charge of coordination between the Territorial Defence and the police, the JNA had its own command and was supposed to leave on the 19th from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they were not able to because their barracks were under siege. Everybody knows that I had no jurisdiction over it and you could see that from the transcript produced here. If I could have called up some commanders who would report to me, as Mr. Brown seemed to imply, that would be incorrect. I could have called as a private person to find out what was going on, but it wouldn't have been an official inquiry from a superior to a subordinate. It was not about the line of command, and you can see that from the papers. Mr. Brown probably didn't have available to him the facts that we know and he drew the wrong conclusion. Why wouldn't the speaker of the assembly call up people he knew to inquire? Why wouldn't I do that, even if I occupied a lower office than I did? I was interested in that area but I was interested in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina too. It doesn't mean that I have any jurisdiction over anything or that I have a position of superiority, which makes the conclusion drawn by Mr. Brown completely incorrect. He probably would change his mind too, if he had been able to read those conclusions and familiarise himself with the documents. But he must have based his conclusions on something different, or maybe he had a prior theory that he was trying to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we take the break, perhaps I should also ask you, so far as the last conversation is concerned, that is the one between you and Mr. Grkovic on the 27th of May, that in fact was played to this Court at page 6290 of the transcript, during the evidence of Mr. Kljuic, and he simply said, the whole thing having been played, that this is indicative of your knowledge of the situation on the ground. Presumably your answer to that is the same as you've just given in relation to my question concerning Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had known, I wouldn't have been calling this man. I called in order to find out, to check those reports, the random information I was getting from all sides. But let me tell you one thing: As far as this agreement between the Presidency and the JNA was signed, I have a copy of that. It should have been signed by Mr. Kljuic. I think it was signed by him. And it should have been honoured. I'm not blaming Mr. Kljuic, but his side and the other side violated the agreement. We can see that from various sources. Both Mr. Abdic and Mr. Kljuic are the kind of people who would honour agreements they signed but it was local people who attacked this column, not giving a damn about what the Presidency decided. You can see that from the book of Mr. Loncarevic when he writes that somebody was saying, Well, they will be angry with us if we take the weapons, and another person replies, What do we care? We just take the weapons. I'm not blaming anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we are about at the break. My recollection doesn't tell me whether this agreement is in evidence, yes or no. That's the agreement between, from what I understand, between the JNA and Presidency on the withdrawal from the Marshal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know off-hand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please find out and see whether there is any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in evidence. I can provide it. I just don't have it here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the parties consider, because it makes -- let me say the following. It could -- it could be relevant to know whether knowledge of military matters on the ground are directly related to an agreement which was concluded, not by just the military but where government or at least civilian authorities were involved in such an agreement, or whether this knowledge was there if there was not any previous civilian involvement in the situation that arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Neither Mr. Harmon nor I have any specific recollection that that document is in evidence. We can check on the break but essentially at this point our recollection is the same as my learned friend's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would the parties consider whether it would be -- whether it would assist the Chamber to have this, the copy of such an agreement in evidence. Then we'll have a break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, there was one issue pending in relation to Exhibit P64A, tab 698, the minutes from a meeting of the National Security Council and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 28th of April. There was a problem with one word, being illegible in paragraph 10 of these minutes. Meanwhile, and -- the parties have consulted their language experts, and have agreed on a -- how to read this paragraph, and with the always appreciated assistance of CLSS, now a new translation has been provided. Based on this agreement on what that word is in B/C/S, the translation is as follows: "Ten: Suggestion adopted on the need to inform the Crisis Staffs more fully about opinions, proposals, and information available to the public, and on the Crisis Staff informing the government." That's the new translation. The Prosecution is invited to file a new, corrected translation of P64A, tab 698.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One additional matter, Your Honour, related to the closed-session or private-session discussion earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe I can address it without the need to go into private session. And I would indicate to the Court that the item discussed has been provided to the Registrar, who has it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber observes that this is the second time that a mistake was made, which is not -- which is not how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is pointing at me. I think he has something he would like to mention to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it has got nothing to do with the last observation made by Mr. Tieger, then we can remain in open session. Otherwise we would have to go into private session. Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be careful not to do anything wrong in terms of public sessions. I just have December 2003, what the Prosecution provided. I don't have this particular date. So could I please have a copy of what you received just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- before Your Honours came into court, Mr. Sladojevic showed me a CD, so clearly some service has been made on the Defence, but the problem remains the same, of not contacting Mr. Krajisnik. If the Prosecution could produce another CD, that would be the easiest solution. If not, I suppose we will have to try and copy the one we have been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, we will be happy to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that being resolved, we can continue. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the Bench in front of you is an additional intercept. This in fact is P625. I wasn't going to ask Mr. Krajisnik about it. Could he be given a copy, please? Because it's not in the bundle. This was introduced as a contextual exhibit, after or in the course of the evidence of a protected witness. As far as we can see, it has never been alluded to at all during the course of this trial. Your Honour, again it's in the light of the questions that Your Honour asked of Mr. Krajisnik that I'm now bringing this to his attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a conversation on the same day, 21st of April 1992, between you and someone called an unidentified male. From the Vraca local community, he says rather pointedly, when you, Mr. Krajisnik, ask him whether he's a member of the Crisis Staff. And on the second page you ask whether they, "Can they withdraw?" And he said, "Well, they tried, they went down there to try to get those men out of encirclement." Goes on, there was great treason there. You asked who betrayed. And he says, "Well, who knows? They just welcomed them. They simply ran into fire." Bearing in mind what you've already said about the situation in Vraca, does this help refresh your memory or recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a sequel to the conversation I had with Mr. Garic. I tried for some reasons to make some additional checks and I tried to reach him but he had by then probably left that locality so somebody answered phone. I didn't even check who it was. And I asked him about the situation there and he described it the way we said earlier on, that somebody got there, that there was some kind of treason, words to that effect. That man is probably trying to justify the persons who took this ill conceived action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move one, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one clarifying question. A couple of times in these telephone conversations people are talking about down and down there. Should this be understood to be Vraca a little bit elevated from the Grbavica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now going to turn to the two conversations that the Defence are -- have been plead aware of that contain exchanges between the witness and Ratko Mladic. Both have been exhibited. One has previously been played. Because of their obvious importance in the case, I intend to have both played and then ask Mr. Krajisnik about them. The first is one on the 24th of May of 1992. It's our tab 185. It bears exhibit number P154, tab 33. As far as we are aware it's never been referred to at all in the evidence previously. Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A number should be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It has a number, Your Honour. It has a number. It's just never been referred to. It's part of a large batch of Babic intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it has, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that please be played?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have any copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look. Which numbers are they in your bundle?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 185, in the left-hand margin. I thought these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have, it's listed here 184 and then it jumps to 186 on the index.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I hadn't spotted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see, with the front page is intercepts involving MK, and they are -- 183 and 185 are not on the index or the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sladojevic can put it up on the screen in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that would best --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that it is usually impossible to actually interpret these intercepts. We can barely hear them and it is very fast. We agreed earlier on that we would read out the written translations provided to us. If we do not have a written translation, we cannot read it out and we cannot hear most of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, therefore, even if the B/C/S version would be on the ELMO, then speech would be too quick, so perhaps you provide and leave it to a later moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct. I'm not going to deal with either of these. I'm going to move on to a completely different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's appreciated. I had another gotten about that it's not just the B/C/S text not being available but also that the interpreters would need, in order to do their job properly, the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I thank the interpreters for pointing that out. Could I be given one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you can put the intercept bundle away. We will return to that tomorrow morning. I'm going to ask you about a discrete and completely separate topic. And that really involves the departure of the Muslims from Pale. This was ostensibly dealt with in this Court by the evidence of Mr. Crncalo who was a Muslim inhabitant of the town at that time. He in particular described a series of meetings involving the president of the municipality, and also Malko Koroman, the chief of police that culminated in the departure of the Muslims. At one of these meetings, he described Mr. Koljevic as being present and saying, "It does not matter that you want to live with us. The Serbs don't want to go on living with you." What was your knowledge of these events and the difficulties, if any, that the local Muslims were having?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surname I heard was wrong. And I'm afraid that this might have been a protected witness. I know the person's name. I know who spoke about this. But the last name is quite different. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's quite different, we do not even need a redaction. But even then, Witness, let's first turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, educate me, please; how shall I be pronouncing this gentleman's name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness's name was Sulejman, Crncalo, Crncalo. Could the interpreters please spell it out?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters's note, C-r-n-c, with a diacritic, a-l-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The question I asked in relation to him, a few moments ago, was a summary, involved a summary of his description of events prior to his departure, events involving the president of the municipality, Mr. Koroman, and at one point, Mr. Koljevic. And my question to you was how much you knew about these events.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When that was happening, I did not know when it was that the Muslims had left Pale. When the process was over, I found out. I only heard about it during a conversation when they expressed their intention of wanting to leave Pale. I showed you where Kikinda was. This entire activity was conducted by the municipality, and I assert before this gathering that the Muslims left voluntarily and that there is a decision of the municipality that there is their request, there is their list, there is a record from the municipal assembly when some people voiced their opposition in terms of them leaving, and the then Muslim units had committed a true massacre over the territorials from Pale and over 50 men got killed then or I don't know the exact number. So it was then that they wanted to leave Pale at any cost. As for all the documents that came after this testimony, they were collected and there are several statements from people from Pale who we did not manage to bring here, but that were verified. This was the president of the municipality, members of the Crisis Staff, and so on and so forth. Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Karadzic, or I did not participate in this. On the contrary, this was a totally unnecessary thing done by them because politically it was bad later, and this man, and I assert that, and I'll show you that, he was highly uninformed. There is a contract on the exchange of the house that he had signed. His house in Pale was returned. There is this entire documentation, and I can give you an answer to everyone of your questions based on all the investigations carried out, if I can put it that way. But at that time, when this happened, the entire municipality was so unhappy. No one wanted them to leave. On the contrary, they left because they could have been stopped only by force, and that would have gone against the grain of our principles, making it impossible for someone to freely decide on where they would go. So I ask you, please, since I was in Pale, I'm aware of each and every detail now, and I have all this documentation for you so that you can have the true picture. So in response to your question, at first I knew that there was a wish on their part. I was not aware of the process itself, as it evolved when they made a request to the assembly -- to the municipal assembly and so on but it was only later that I found out that they had actually left. That was it. Not only me, but Mr. Koljevic and everybody else. They left. They took whatever they could take. Your Honours, this man did not sell his house or exchange it. There were these contracts on safekeeping houses. You take care of my house on the other side and I take care of your house. And this is a contract that had been certified and the man's house was returned to him. Obviously this witness was a bit less informed because his brother made a statement that was quite different. There is also a statement made by a Muslim lady who stayed there throughout the war and she talked about how she fared. So it would be very useful to look into this entire matter and to call some witnesses from Pale itself so that they could say specifically what happened. There are several witnesses who are there, and you can choose who you would like to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that there is room for considerable latitude in an examination of this nature. However, when Mr. Krajisnik begins to cite alleged statements that are not before the Court, begins to marshal evidence that's not going to be before the Court, and weave them into his examination, that's where we have to draw the line. I certainly don't blame my learned friend. I don't think that he attempted to elicit that and I accept that Mr. Krajisnik is not so familiar with the process that he may understand the problem but I think at this point, Your Honour, that's a line that should be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it either should have been raised in cross-examination or it should have been put to the witness at that time under Rule 89(H)?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There are a variety of other ways of dealing with it. This would not the proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of the points that Mr. Tieger has just raised I was going to attempt to clarify with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Krajisnik, you referred twice to the fact that there were witnesses from Pale who could say specifically what happened. And you also said that -- excuse me a moment. I quote, "We did not manage to bring here." Clearly referring to those witnesses. As far as you are concerned, why have those witnesses not come before this Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, now we are moving in a completely different direction and I -- that's not a relevant matter for purposes of the objection I made. If there is some intention afoot to broaden the nature of the evidence before the Court, then it needs to be addressed directly. My objection is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say under those circumstances to say it very -- perhaps in an unconventional way, then Mr. Krajisnik should be in the position of the accused again and the parties should not through a witness first discuss what latitude there would be to introduce any further evidence and then the second question is whether it could be done by this witness. Is that what you had in mind? Or, of course, I'm not that familiar with how to resolve these matters in a fairly adversarial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps before my learned friend replies, my response was going to be a rhetorical one: What is wrong with that question, the question that I have just asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I raised an objection. Now, what I understood counsel to be doing, was to be laying some kind of foundation for making-- for the reasons why, not even for the justification for, legal justification for, but for the motivation for trying to use Mr. Krajisnik as some sort of summary witness for information that was otherwise not going to be before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't understand it to be that Mr. Krajisnik was introduced as a summary witness but rather to find out what the procedural consequences should be from the fact that if there were good reasons to believe that these witnesses could not be called to appear in this Court, and then to later perhaps discuss what the consequences would be, but first, just to establish what Mr. Krajisnik knows about the impossibility of those witnesses to appear before this court, and not any further, and not to replace their potential --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- evidence, by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's understood like that, would you still object, Mr. Tieger? We would limit it clearly to: Does Mr. Krajisnik know, did he contact them and -- or did they die, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think an objection could be made. I think nevertheless the Defence wishes to bring that information before the court. It seems to me the Court wishes to hear that limited information, and on that basis I won't stand in the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed, Mr. Josse, in accordance with that small corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we don't want to know what these people would have said or might say, were they to provide statements or were they to come here. We simply want to know what you understand to be the reasons the Defence have not called them.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reply, but I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me just a brief comment on what just transpired, to assist the Trial Chamber of course. The Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very much a procedural issue that comes up which is left in the lands of counsel, so you may respond to the question put to you by Mr. Josse, whether you're aware of the reasons why the Defence did not call these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will answer. The Defence did not call these witnesses because they did not have time. There are certified statements, a number of them, and one of them was ready and willing to come on several occasions but simply didn't fit with the schedule. That's Mr. Sarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's all you need to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's due to time reasons that these witnesses were not called. That reminds me of a lot of submissions and quite a few decisions taken by this Chamber and also the emphasis this Chamber has put on whether to use the time for preparation or to present evidence in court. I don't have to revisit all that but that comes into our minds at this moment without drawing any conclusions at this very moment. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, you made me a promise, if I may just remind you so that I can avoid errors in my further testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the promise was, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you remember, when I sat at the other Bench, you said that if I have knowledge of a document or an event or anything at all that could be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and everybody else, that I should produce it, and that -- that was some sort of privilege of mine. Maybe I cross that line from time to time with the best of intentions just to let you know what I know. Everybody keeps interrupting me. I can't finish one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be a good reason why Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The good reason is, I was going to ask you this very question. That was going to be my next question which was, you had referred in the long, substantive answer you gave explaining your knowledge or lack of knowledge in relation to the departure of these people, to documents. I was going to invite you to bring them here tomorrow morning. Any problem with that? It's a question to you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse invites to you bring them tomorrow morning and ask whether you have any problem in doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They have all the documents, and so do I. And if they don't have them, I'll try to locate them. No problem. All right, I'll try to find all those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we will do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I foresee -- could I just inquire at this moment, the last minute, what are we going to expect? I mean, are we talking about decisions of the Crisis Staff or are we talking about statements of witnesses? Because that makes quite a difference for me. And perhaps also for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have a file in this building that says "Pale" on it. I think the documents in that file fall into the category of the former rather than the latter. However, I need to check and -- but I am fairly certain about is that most of them are untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which makes the issue not easier -- any easier because very often we know more or less what to expect from a document by just reading the title, that -- well, I would very much like, Mr. Josse, you to use part of the afternoon discussing the matter, because this creates -- well, could I say a procedural novelty, if witness statements would be introduced by the accused as a witness, where 92 bis has not been used, the witness has not been called. I'm talking about if there were any witness statements in there. And then untranslated brought to our attention, that at least creates a situation which I have not seen described before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me make life a little bit simple. I don't know what course Mr. Krajisnik would like me to undertake or any course he might wish to undertake himself but at this stage of the case, I certainly do not intend to do that. Counsel are not going to introduce statements from witnesses via Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, Mr. Krajisnik, if you have documents, you may have perceived from this discussion that it would create at least a very complex and difficult procedural situation if the documents you would find this evening would be witness statements, and you referred to statements of witnesses earlier so there is a fair chance that there would be a strong opposition and I'm perhaps not -- my guess is not far from what we could expect, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that could create quite a lot of problems. If, however, there are other documents, let's just assume that any municipal body has taken any decision in which it invited all the citizens to discuss exchange of property, that might be a totally different matter and then we are in the area of what I would call the kind of documents we found in Prosecution dossiers as well. Then there still remains the issue whether the witnesses should have been confronted with that material at an earlier stage but if we come to that, if we come to that bridge, we will cross it. Or stop before the bridge. I don't know what it will be. But I think it would be good that the parties would communicate this afternoon to see more or less what they could expect from each other tomorrow and see to what extent problems could be resolved in a consensual way already. This having said, I've lost my little note on that -- we'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Krajisnik, but not until after I've instructed you not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given. You might not even have time, being very busy perhaps this evening, in finding your documents, but this is my instruction for you. We will adjourn to tomorrow, 9.00, same courtroom, and the parties are informed that the Registrar has sent updated lists of exhibits to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
